subject: ela
description: Students write narratives that develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences. They engage and orient the reader by establishing a context and introducing a narrator and characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally and logically; use narrative techniques such as dialogue, pacing, and description to develop experiences, events, and characters; use a variety of transition words, phrases, and clauses to convey sequence and signal shifts from one time frame or setting to another; use precise words and phrases, relevant descriptive details, and sensory language to convey experiences and events; and provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects on the narrated experiences or events. Every item embeds the full sentence, paragraph, or short model passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Engage and orient the reader by establishing a context, point of view, and introducing a narrator and/or characters
Organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally and logically from beginning to end
Use dialogue to develop characters and advance the action, including correct punctuation of quoted speech
Use pacing and description to develop experiences, events, and characters (slowing down for key moments, speeding through minor ones)
Use transition words, phrases, and clauses to convey sequence and signal shifts in time frame or setting
Use precise words, relevant descriptive details, and sensory language (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) to convey experiences vividly
Provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects on the narrated experiences or events

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the strongest narrative opening
problemArchetypes.example: Read these two openings for a story about a first day at a new school. Opening A: 'I went to my new school. It was big.' Opening B: 'My sneakers squeaked down the empty hallway as the late bell echoed behind me, and forty unfamiliar faces turned toward the door.' Which opening better engages and orients the reader, and why? Answer: Opening B, because it establishes context (a hallway, a late bell), introduces the narrator's situation, and uses sensory detail to pull the reader in.

problemArchetypes.name: Order events into a logical sequence
problemArchetypes.example: Read these four events from a story, listed out of order: (1) Tomas finally reeled the fish onto the dock. (2) Tomas woke before sunrise and packed his tackle box. (3) Tomas felt a sudden, hard tug on the line. (4) Tomas cast his line into the still gray water. Put the events in the order that unfolds naturally. Answer: 2, 4, 3, 1, because the story moves from preparation, to casting, to the bite, to landing the fish.

problemArchetypes.name: Add or improve dialogue to develop a character
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'Mara was nervous about the audition.' Choose the revision that uses dialogue to show her nervousness instead of telling it. Answer: 'Mara peeked around the curtain and whispered, "What if I forget every line the second I walk out there?"' because the spoken words reveal her fear through her own voice.

problemArchetypes.name: Select the best transition to signal a shift in time or setting
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage: 'We searched the attic for hours and found nothing. ____ we climbed down, dusty and discouraged, and noticed the loose floorboard in the hall.' Which transition best signals the shift? Answer: 'Finally,' because it conveys the sequence and marks the move to a new moment and place.

problemArchetypes.name: Replace vague wording with precise, sensory description
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'The food at the fair was good.' Choose the revision with the most precise, sensory detail. Answer: 'The funnel cake was warm and crisp, dusted with powdered sugar that melted on my tongue,' because it uses specific nouns and appeals to taste and touch.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose a conclusion that reflects on the experience
problemArchetypes.example: Read the story ending options for a narrative about losing a championship game. Ending A: 'Then we got on the bus and went home. The end.' Ending B: 'On the quiet bus ride home, I realized that the score on the board would fade, but the way my team never stopped fighting was something I would carry for a long time.' Which conclusion follows from and reflects on the events? Answer: Ending B, because it grows out of the narrated experience and offers a reflection on what it meant.

Easy.description: A single short sentence or a two-line stimulus (roughly 8 to 20 words) embedded in the item. The task is to identify a single narrative element or pick the clearly stronger of two short options: spotting a sensory detail, choosing the more engaging opening, identifying a transition word, or selecting the line of dialogue. Only one technique is tested and the better choice is obvious.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or a pair of short lines included in the prompt
Tests exactly one technique (opening, transition, dialogue, sensory detail, or sequence of 3 events)
Identify-level task: pick the stronger option or name the element
The contrast between correct and incorrect choices is clear and direct

Medium.description: A short paragraph or a four to five event sequence (roughly 25 to 55 words) embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: ordering events logically, choosing the revision that best develops a character through dialogue or pacing, replacing flat wording with precise sensory language, or selecting the transition that signals a shift in time frame or setting. The student weighs several plausible options, not an obvious right and wrong.
constraints: Stimulus is a short paragraph or a 4 to 5 event list included in the prompt
Tests sequencing, pacing, dialogue development, or transitions between settings or time frames
Analyze-level task: choose or arrange the best version among close options
Distractors are plausible partial improvements that fix one issue but miss another

Hard.description: A multi-paragraph model passage or a full short narrative excerpt (roughly 60 to 120 words) embedded in the item that the student must read closely. The task requires evaluation: judging which conclusion best follows from and reflects on the whole narrative, identifying the single revision that most improves a passage's pacing or coherence, explaining why an event sequence breaks down, or selecting the ending that ties together an established context, narrator, and theme. Requires inference about the writer's intent and the story's overall arc.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-paragraph or full short-narrative excerpt included in the prompt
Tests how techniques work together across a whole piece (orientation through conclusion)
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision, conclusion, or coherence fix and justify it
Requires inference about narrator intent, theme, and the complete event arc

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes a narrative opening should simply state the topic or setting flatly rather than orient and engage the reader
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'This is a story about my summer. It was fun.' as the strongest opening instead of one that establishes context and draws the reader in

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses telling about a feeling with showing it through action and dialogue
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'Mara was very nervous' over a revision that reveals the nervousness through her words or trembling hands, assuming naming the emotion is the best technique

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student orders events by which sounds most exciting or important rather than by the natural cause-and-effect time sequence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Places the dramatic climax (landing the fish) before the setup (packing the tackle box) because it seems like the best hook

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a transition word that does not match the relationship between events, treating all transitions as interchangeable connectors
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'For example' or 'In addition' to signal a shift to a new moment in time where 'Later' or 'The next morning' is needed

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student equates more or longer words with more precise description and overlooks specific, sensory detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a wordy but vague revision like 'The food was extremely very good and amazing' over one with concrete sensory detail

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks any sentence that stops the action is an acceptable conclusion and that a conclusion need not connect to the rest of the story
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'Then we went home. The end.' as the conclusion instead of one that follows from and reflects on the narrated events

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats dialogue as decoration that can be dropped in anywhere, with no regard for whether it advances the action or reveals character, and ignores correct punctuation of quoted speech
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects off-topic or mispunctuated dialogue such as 'She said hi.' over spoken lines that develop the character and move the story forward
